# Foundations of Data Science ZZSC9001

## 0 · R/RStudio foundations

### 0.1 · Vectors, indexing and functions

**Concept**

R evaluates expressions and stores their results in named objects. Vector operations apply to each element. RStudio is an IDE; R is the computing language.

**Example**

Three electricity customers use 100, 200 and 300 kWh; the tariff is $20 plus $0.30/kWh.

```{r}
options(width=95, digits=5)
usage <- c(100, 200, 300)
bill <- function(kwh, rate=0.30, fixed=20) {
  fixed + rate * kwh
}
print(bill(usage))
print(usage[usage >= 200])
print(usage[1])
stopifnot(identical(bill(usage), c(50,80,110)))
cat(R.version.string, "\n")
```

### 0.2 · Tables, factors, missing values and grouped means

**Concept**

A data frame has one observation per row and one variable per column. Factors represent categories, not arbitrary numerical scores.

**Example**

Four customer records contain one missing usage value.

```{r}
customers <- data.frame(id=1:4, plan=factor(c("A","A","B","B")),kwh=c(100,200,300,NA))
print(customers)
print(is.na(customers$kwh))
print("------------")
print(c(raw_mean=mean(customers$kwh), observed_mean=mean(customers$kwh,na.rm=TRUE)))
print("------------")
print(tapply(customers$kwh, customers$plan, mean, na.rm=TRUE))
print("------------")
print(customers[!is.na(customers$kwh) & customers$plan=="A", , drop=FALSE])
```

## 1 · Probability and randomness — Statistics Quiz / Final

### 1.1 · Events, complements, unions and counting

**Concept**

For events A and B, P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Counting favourable outcomes works directly only for equally likely outcomes.

**Example**

Among six equally likely order outcomes, A={2,4,6} and B={4,5,6}.

```{r}
omega <- 1:6; A <- c(2,4,6); B <- c(4,5,6)
pA <- length(A)/length(omega); pB <- length(B)/length(omega)
pAB <- length(intersect(A,B))/length(omega)
print(c(A=pA, B=pB, intersection=pAB, union=pA+pB-pAB, complement_A=1-pA))
print("------------")
print(choose(5,2))
stopifnot(abs((pA+pB-pAB)-length(union(A,B))/6)<1e-12)
```

### 1.2 · Conditional probability and independence

**Concept**

Conditioning changes the reference population. P(churn|complaint) divides by customers with complaints.

**Example**

1,000 customers: 60 complaint/churn, 140 complaint/stay, 40 no-complaint/churn, 760 no-complaint/stay.

```{r}
tab <- matrix(c(60,140,40,760),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,
              dimnames=list(complaint=c("yes","no"),outcome=c("churn","stay")))
print(tab)
print("------------")
print(c(p_churn=sum(tab[,"churn"])/sum(tab),
        p_churn_given_complaint=tab["yes","churn"]/sum(tab["yes",]),
        p_complaint_given_churn=tab["yes","churn"]/sum(tab[,"churn"])))
print(prop.table(tab,margin=1))
```

### 1.3 · Bayes and the base rate

**Concept**

Posterior probability = prior × likelihood / total evidence probability.

**Example**

A fraud detector has sensitivity .8 and false-positive rate .05; only 1% of payments are fraudulent.

```{r}
prior <- .01; sensitivity <- .8; false_positive <- .05
true_alert <- prior*sensitivity
false_alert <- (1-prior)*false_positive
posterior <- true_alert/(true_alert+false_alert)
print(c(expected_true_alerts=10000*true_alert, expected_false_alerts=10000*false_alert, posterior=posterior))
print(c(review_value=120*posterior-8))
```

Even though our system has an 80% success rate, if an alarm goes off, there is only a 13.9% chance it is real. The remaining 86.1% are false alarms. This paradox is known as the Base Rate Fallacy.

### 1.4 · PMFs, expectation, variance and covariance

**Concept**

A PMF assigns probabilities to discrete values. E[X]=Σxp(x); Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])²]. Covariance describes joint co-movement.

**Example**

A support case costs $0, $100 or $200 with probabilities .2, .5, .3.

```{r}
cost <- c(0,100,200); p <- c(.2,.5,.3)
mu <- sum(cost*p); variance <- sum((cost-mu)^2*p)
print(c(mean=mu, variance=variance, sd=sqrt(variance)))
print(c(var_scaled=4*variance, mean_shifted=2*mu+10))
x <- c(1,2,3,4); y <- c(2,5,5,8)
print(c(sample_cov=cov(x,y), correlation=cor(x,y)))
stopifnot(sum(p)==1, variance==4900)
```

### 1.5 · Distribution functions: d, p, q and r

**Concept**

Bernoulli models one binary outcome; binomial counts independent equal-probability trials; Poisson models counts under a constant-rate independent-increments model; normal models a continuous symmetric variable.

**Example**

Calculate exactly 3 of 10 customers churning at p=.2, more than 2 arrivals at mean 4, and a normal service-time interval.

```{r}
print(c(exactly3=dbinom(3,size=10,prob=.2),
        more_than2=pbinom(2,10,.2,lower.tail=FALSE),
        poisson_over2=ppois(2,lambda=4,lower.tail=FALSE)))
print(c(normal_90_to110=pnorm(110,100,15)-pnorm(90,100,15),
        normal_95th=qnorm(.95,100,15)))
set.seed(101); print(rbinom(8,size=1,prob=.2))
```

### 1.6 · Monte Carlo and the law of large numbers

**Concept**

Simulation estimates a probability by repeated random outcomes. Monte Carlo SE describes uncertainty from a finite simulation.

**Example**

Estimate the probability of at least three churners in ten independent customers.

```{r}
set.seed(102)
B <- 10000
counts <- rbinom(B,10,.2)
hit <- counts>=3
estimate <- mean(hit)
mc_se <- sqrt(estimate*(1-estimate)/B)
print(c(simulated=estimate, exact=pbinom(2,10,.2,lower.tail=FALSE), MC_SE=mc_se))
running <- cumsum(hit)/seq_along(hit)
plot(running,type="l",xlab="Simulation count",ylab="Estimated probability")
abline(h=pbinom(2,10,.2,lower.tail=FALSE),col="red",lty=2)
```

```{r}
set.seed(103)
means1 <- replicate(4000,mean(rexp(1,rate=.1)))
means50 <- replicate(4000,mean(rexp(50,rate=.1)))
print(rbind(n1=c(mean=mean(means1),sd=sd(means1),theory_SE=10),
            n50=c(mean=mean(means50),sd=sd(means50),theory_SE=10/sqrt(50))))
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(means1,main="Individual times",xlab="Minutes",col="lightblue")
hist(means50,main="Means of 50",xlab="Minutes",col="lightgreen")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

## 2 · Inferential statistics

### 2.1 · Estimator, SD, SE and confidence interval

**Concept**

A parameter describes a population; an estimator is a rule applied to a sample. SD measures individual spread; SE measures estimator uncertainty.

**Example**

Five independent normally distributed customer bills are 80,90,100,110,120 dollars. Estimate their population mean.

```{r}
bills <- c(80,90,100,110,120)
n <- length(bills)
m <- mean(bills)
s <- sd(bills)
se <- s/sqrt(n)
ci <- m + c(-1,1)*qt(.975,df=n-1)*se
print(c(n=n,mean=m,SD=s,SE=se,lower=ci[1],upper=ci[2]))
print(t.test(bills)$conf.int)
stopifnot(max(abs(ci-t.test(bills)$conf.int))<1e-10)
```

### 2.2 · Hypothesis tests, p-values and CI duality

**Concept**

A p-value measures how extreme the observed statistic is under a specified null model. It does not give the probability that the null is true.

**Example**

Test whether average bills equal $95 using the previous sample.

```{r}
test <- t.test(bills,mu=95,alternative="two.sided")
t_manual <- (mean(bills)-95)/(sd(bills)/sqrt(length(bills)))
p_manual <- 2*pt(-abs(t_manual),df=length(bills)-1)
print(c(t=t_manual,p=p_manual,reject_at_05=p_manual<.05))
print(test$conf.int)
stopifnot(abs(p_manual-test$p.value)<1e-12)
```
